title: What is session-based authentication — server stores session in memory/DB, sends session ID in cookie, stateful — and what are its problems (scalability, CSRF vulnerability, sticky sessions)?

s1_definition.profdef: Session-based authentication is a stateful scheme in which, after a successful login, the server creates a session record (holding the user's identity and attributes) and stores it server-side in memory or a database. It then sends only an opaque session identifier to the client, usually in a cookie. On every later request the client sends that cookie back, and the server looks up the session to recover the identity. Because the authoritative state lives on the server, the server must keep and share that state across all instances.
s1_definition.analogy: When Rajesh enters National Bank of India, the receptionist writes his full details in a big register and hands him a small token numbered "42". Every time Rajesh approaches a counter he just shows token 42, and the staff flips to page 42 in the register to see who he is. The token itself is meaningless — all the real information sits in the bank's register. The problem is: if Rajesh goes to a different branch that does not have the same register, nobody knows who token 42 is.
s1_definition.oneliner: The session ID is a claim check; the real identity stays in the server's cloakroom.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Session-based authentication is a stateful scheme in which, after a successful login, the server creates a session record (holding the user's identity and attributes) and stores it server-side in memory or a database. It then sends only an opaque session identifier to the client, usually in a cookie. On every later request the client sends that cookie back, and the server looks up the session to recover the identity. Because the authoritative state lives on the server, the server must keep and share that state across all instances.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** When Rajesh enters National Bank of India, the receptionist writes his full details in a big register and hands him a small token numbered "42". Every time Rajesh approaches a counter he just shows token 42, and the staff flips to page 42 in the register to see who he is. The token itself is meaningless — all the real information sits in the bank's register. The problem is: if Rajesh goes to a different branch that does not have the same register, nobody knows who token 42 is.

**One line to remember:** The session ID is a claim check; the real identity stays in the server's cloakroom.

sections.s2_technical:
On login the server creates a session, for example `HttpSession session = request.getSession(true); session.setAttribute("user", "rajesh");`. The container generates a session ID like `JSESSIONID=3F2A...` and returns it as a `Set-Cookie` header. The browser automatically sends it back on every subsequent request, and the server resolves identity with `request.getSession(false).getAttribute("user")`.

The first problem is scalability and sticky sessions. Because the session lives in one server's memory, if you run three instances behind a load balancer, a user authenticated on instance A will not be recognized on instance B. Teams work around this with sticky sessions (the load balancer always routes a user to the same instance) or by externalizing sessions into a shared store like Redis, for example with Spring Session: `@EnableRedisHttpSession`. Sticky sessions hurt failover and even load distribution; a shared store adds a network hop and a new dependency.

The second problem is CSRF vulnerability. Because the cookie is sent automatically by the browser on every request to the domain, a malicious site can trick the browser into firing a money-transfer request that silently carries the victim's valid cookie. The defenses are a CSRF token that the attacker cannot read, and the `SameSite` cookie attribute. A senior nuance: session-based auth is actually very convenient for server-rendered monoliths and allows instant server-side revocation (just delete the session), which stateless JWTs cannot do easily.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — Rajesh logs into the National Bank of India web portal. The bank needs to remember across many page clicks that this browser belongs to Rajesh, without asking for his password on every click. This is exactly how a session works — the server stores Rajesh's identity once and hands back a small session ID cookie that stands in for it.

Problem 2 — The bank runs three identical servers for high traffic. Rajesh logs in on server one, but his next click is routed to server two, which has never heard of his session ID. Suddenly he is logged out. This is exactly the sticky-session and scalability problem — server-held state does not automatically exist on the other servers unless we share it.

Our mini-project builds a `SessionStore` (simulating server memory), a `SessionAuthService` that creates and validates sessions, and a demo that shows a working lookup on the same server and a failed lookup when the request lands on a different server instance without a shared store.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a login for user "rajesh", then two identity lookups — one on server A, one on server B.

Step 1: `login("rajesh")` runs on server A. A random session ID is generated and a `SessionData` holding "rajesh" and a 30-minute expiry is stored in server A's in-memory map. The session ID is returned as the cookie value. The real identity lives only in server A's memory.

Step 2: `whoAmI(sessionId)` runs on server A. The map lookup finds the `SessionData`, it is not expired, and "rajesh" is returned. Everything works because the request stayed on the same instance.

Step 3: The next request is routed by the load balancer to server B. `whoAmI(sessionId)` runs against server B's separate in-memory map, which never stored this session. The lookup returns null, so the user appears logged out. This demonstrates the scalability and sticky-session problem.

Step 4: The fix (shown in config) is to move `SessionStore` into shared Redis so both A and B read the same session — at the cost of an extra network hop and dependency.

```text
2026-10-31 22:35:00.010 INFO    [SessionDemo] Login OK on server A, cookie JSESSIONID=9f2c-...
2026-10-31 22:35:00.012 INFO    [SessionDemo] server A resolves session to: rajesh
2026-10-31 22:35:00.013 SEVERE  [SessionDemo] server B cannot find session 9f2c-... -> user appears logged out (sticky-session / scalability problem)
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  Client login: POST /login {user: rajesh}
    │
    ▼
  Server A  (in-memory SessionStore)
    │ create session 9f2c → {rajesh, exp+30m}
    │ Set-Cookie: JSESSIONID=9f2c; HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Strict
    ▼
  Client stores cookie, sends it on every request
    │
    ├─ routed back to Server A           ├─ routed to Server B (no shared store)
    │  lookup 9f2c ✓ → rajesh            │  lookup 9f2c ✗ → null
    ▼                                     ▼
  200 OK (recognized)                    401/redirect to login (lost session)
```

```text
  │ + whoAmI(id): String      │        └──────────┬───────────────┘
  │ + logout(id): void        │                   │ contains

                                     │   expiresAt, isExpired()} │
                                     └──────────────────────────┘

  State: ACTIVE ──timeout/logout──→ EXPIRED/REMOVED (lookup → null)

  Contract for whoAmI(id):
    Post: returns username if session exists & not expired, else null
    Note: logout() gives INSTANT revocation (delete session) — a JWT cannot
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Session-based authentication is a stateful approach where, after login, the server creates a session record holding the user's identity and keeps it server-side, in memory or a database, while sending only an opaque session identifier back to the client in a cookie. On every later request the browser automatically returns the cookie, and the server looks up the session to recover who the user is. The important point is that the real state lives on the server; the cookie is just a claim check.

In my banking project, this worked beautifully for a single server, but the moment we scaled to three instances behind a load balancer we hit the classic problems. The first is scalability and sticky sessions: because the session sits in one instance's memory, a user who logs in on instance A is not recognized on instance B unless the load balancer pins them to A, which hurts failover and even load distribution. We solved it by externalizing sessions into Redis with Spring Session, which trades a little latency for shared state.

The second problem is CSRF. Because the cookie is sent automatically on every request, a malicious page can trick the browser into firing a transfer request that silently carries the victim's valid session cookie. We defended against it with a CSRF token the attacker cannot read and the SameSite cookie attribute set to strict, plus HttpOnly and Secure flags.

What I always add is the upside: session auth gives instant server-side revocation. If we detect fraud on Rajesh's account we simply delete his session and he is immediately logged out everywhere, which stateless JWTs make much harder. So I choose sessions for server-rendered banking portals and tokens for stateless microservices, depending on the architecture.
